docs.title: Time-Based Analog-to-Digital Converter
docs.text:
Ongoing Work

This work is currently in progress.

While the architecture and design have been completed, the characterization phase is still ongoing. Additional simulations are required to fully evaluate the system performance.

Furthermore, post-silicon measurements have not yet been conducted, as the fabricated chip has not been received.

This documentation will be updated accordingly once experimental results become available.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This work presents the design and analysis of a Time-Based Analog-to-Digital Converter (TB-ADC) implemented in CMOS technology. The proposed architecture converts an analog input voltage into a time interval, which is subsequently digitized.

\[ V_{in} \rightarrow t_{delay} \rightarrow \text{Digital Code} \]

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
As CMOS technologies scale, voltage headroom decreases, making conventional voltage-domain ADCs less efficient. Time-based architectures offer an alternative by leveraging:

  • Digital-friendly scaling
  • Reduced analog complexity
  • High resolution through temporal quantization

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Voltage-to-Time conversion using a capacitive discharge mechanism
  • Delay-line based Time-to-Digital conversion
  • Thermometer encoding followed by digital processing

docs.title: Global Architecture
docs.text:
The system is composed of three main blocks:

  1. Voltage-to-Time Converter (VTC)
  2. Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC)
  3. Digital Encoding Logic

docs.title: About this Project
docs.text:
This documentation presents the design and analysis of a Time-Based ADC developed within a research-oriented context in analog and mixed-signal circuit design.

The project explores the conversion of analog signals into the time domain, leveraging scalable and CMOS-compatible architectures.

docs.title: Conversion Principle
docs.text:
The TB-ADC performs conversion in two stages:

  1. Analog-to-Time conversion
  2. Time-to-Digital quantization
\[ V_{in} \xrightarrow{\text{VTC}} t_{delay} \xrightarrow{\text{TDC}} D_{out} \]

docs.title: Signal Flow
docs.text:
• The input voltage is sampled
  • A delay proportional to the input is generated
  • This delay propagates through a delay line
  • A thermometer code is produced
  • The code is converted to binary

docs.title: Key Design Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Value Supply Voltage 1.8 V Threshold Voltage \(V_{thr}\) 0.5 V VTC Capacitance 1 pF Discharge Current 1 µA TDC Cells 255 Delay per Cell 5 ns

docs.title: Design Insight
docs.text: The architecture shifts complexity from the analog domain to the time domain, enabling better scalability and robustness in advanced CMOS nodes.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: This work demonstrates the feasibility of a Time-Based ADC using a VTC-TDC architecture.

docs.title: Key Achievements
docs.text:
• Linear voltage-to-time conversion
  • Efficient time quantization
  • Approximate 8-bit resolution

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Reduced analog complexity
  • Excellent scalability
  • Digital-friendly architecture

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Sensitivity to timing jitter
  • Need for calibration
  • PVT variations

docs.title: Future Work
docs.text:

  • INL/DNL characterization
  • Layout optimization

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This section presents a first-order evaluation of the Time-Based ADC based on analytical estimations derived from the design parameters.

At this stage, the fabricated chip has not yet been received, therefore the results rely on schematic-level assumptions and theoretical analysis. The objective is to verify the coherence of the architecture and evaluate its expected performance.

docs.title: VTC Delay Estimation
docs.text:
The VTC generates a delay according to:

\[ t_{delay} = \frac{C}{I}(V_{in} - V_{thr}) \]

Using the design target:

Parameter Value Capacitance \(C\) 100 fF Discharge current \(I\) 100 nA Comparator threshold \(V_{thr}\) 0.5 V

The voltage-to-time gain becomes:

\[ \frac{C}{I} = \frac{100 \times 10^{-15}}{100 \times 10^{-9}} = 1\,\mu s/V \]

Thus:

\[ t_{delay} = 1\,\mu s/V \cdot (V_{in} - 0.5) \]

docs.title: Expected VTC Behavior
docs.text:
\(V_{in}\) \(V_{in}-V_{thr}\) Delay 0.6 V 0.1 V 0.1 µs 0.8 V 0.3 V 0.3 µs 1.0 V 0.5 V 0.5 µs 1.2 V 0.7 V 0.7 µs 1.4 V 0.9 V 0.9 µs 1.5 V 1.0 V 1.0 µs

The delay varies linearly with the input voltage, confirming the expected behavior of the VTC.

docs.title: TDC Dynamic Range
docs.text:
The TDC is implemented with:

  • 255 delay cells
  • \( t_{cell} \approx 5\,ns \)

The full-scale range is:

\[ T_{FS} = 255 \cdot 5\,ns = 1.275\,\mu s \]

This range is well matched to the VTC delay span (~1 µs).

docs.title: ADC Code Estimation
docs.text:
The output code is given by:

\[ D_{out} = \frac{t_{delay}}{t_{cell}} \]

Using:

\[ t_{cell} = 5\,ns \]

we obtain:

\(V_{in}\) \(t_{delay}\) Code 0.6 V 0.1 µs 20 0.8 V 0.3 µs 60 1.0 V 0.5 µs 100 1.2 V 0.7 µs 140 1.4 V 0.9 µs 180 1.5 V 1.0 µs 200

docs.title: Global Transfer Function
docs.text:
Combining VTC and TDC:

\[ D_{out} = \frac{C}{I \cdot t_{cell}}(V_{in} - V_{thr}) \] \[ D_{out} = \frac{1\,\mu s/V}{5\,ns}(V_{in} - 0.5) \] \[ D_{out} = 200 \cdot (V_{in} - 0.5) \]

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
The effective voltage resolution is:

\[ LSB_V = \frac{t_{cell}}{C/I} \] \[ LSB_V = \frac{5\,ns}{1\,\mu s/V} = 5\,mV \]

The equivalent number of bits is:

\[ N_{bits} \approx \log_2(200) \approx 7.6\,bits \]

This corresponds to a near 8-bit resolution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The optimized VTC now generates delays that fully span the TDC range. This ensures that:

  • the delay line is efficiently used
  • the quantization is uniform
  • the ADC achieves a high effective resolution

The system exhibits a linear mapping:

\[ V_{in} \rightarrow t_{delay} \rightarrow D_{out} \]

docs.title: Key Insight
docs.text:
The performance of a Time-Based ADC is primarily determined by the ratio:

\[ \frac{C}{I} \]

By tuning this parameter, the VTC delay can be matched to the TDC range, which is essential to maximize resolution.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The current results are based on first-order estimations and do not include:

  • transistor non-linearities
  • mismatch effects
  • parasitic capacitances
  • comparator offset
  • timing jitter

These effects will impact the final performance.

docs.title: Future Work
docs.text:
Further validation requires:

  • transient simulations of the full system
  • Monte Carlo analysis
  • PVT corner evaluation
  • post-layout extraction
  • silicon measurements

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The analytical results demonstrate that, with the optimized current level, the VTC and TDC are properly matched.

This allows the ADC to achieve:

  • a wide dynamic range
  • a linear transfer function
  • an effective resolution close to 8 bits

The next step is to validate these predictions through simulation and experimental characterization once the fabricated chip becomes available.

docs.title: Global Transfer Function
docs.text:
Combining VTC and TDC:

\[ N = \frac{t_{delay}}{t_{cell}} = \frac{C}{I \cdot t_{cell}} (V_{in} - V_{thr}) \]

docs.title: Gain
docs.text: \[ K = \frac{C}{I \cdot t_{cell}} = \frac{1\,\mu s/V}{5ns} = 200 \]

docs.title: Voltage Resolution
docs.text: \[ LSB_V = \frac{t_{cell}}{C/I} \] \[ LSB_V = \frac{5ns}{1\,\mu s/V} = 5mV \]

docs.title: Effective Resolution
docs.text: \[ N_{bits} = \log_2(255) \approx 8\,bits \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The ADC behaves as a linear voltage-to-code converter.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Scalable architecture
  • Low analog complexity
  • High resolution potential

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) is the digital timing block of the Time-Based ADC. Its role is to convert the time interval generated by the VTC into a digital thermometer code.

\[ t_{delay} \rightarrow D_{out} \]

In this architecture, the TDC is implemented as a delay-line based converter. A START signal propagates through a chain of delay cells, while a STOP signal samples the state of the delay line.

docs.title: Simplified Architecture
docs.text: flowchart LR      START([START]) --> D1[Delay Cell 0]     D1 --> D2[Delay Cell 1]     D2 --> D3[Delay Cell 2]     D3 --> DN[Delay Cell N]      STOP([STOP]) --> L0[Latch 0]     STOP --> L1[Latch 1]     STOP --> L2[Latch 2]     STOP --> LN[Latch N]      D1 --> L0     D2 --> L1     D3 --> L2     DN --> LN      L0 --> TH[tdc_thermo]     L1 --> TH     L2 --> TH     LN --> TH

docs.title: Principle of Operation
docs.text: The TDC operates in two main phases.

docs.title: Propagation Phase
docs.text:
The START signal propagates through the delay line.

If the delay of one cell is \( t_{cell} \), then:

\[ t_k = k \cdot t_{cell} \]

docs.title: Sampling Phase
docs.text:
The STOP signal freezes the delay line.

  • Cells reached by the signal → logic 1
  • Remaining cells → logic 0

This produces a thermometer code:

\[ 1111111100000000 \]

The transition position encodes the time interval.

docs.title: Time Quantization
docs.text: \[ t_{delay} \approx N \cdot t_{cell} \] \[ N \approx \frac{t_{delay}}{t_{cell}} \]

docs.title: Design Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Value Number of cells 255 Cell delay \(t_{cell}\) 5 ns Full-scale range 1.275 µs \[ T_{FS} = 255 \cdot 5\,ns = 1.275\,\mu s \]

docs.title: Relation with the VTC
docs.text:
The VTC is designed to generate:

\[ \frac{C}{I} = 1\,\mu s/V \]

Thus:

\[ t_{delay} = 1\,\mu s/V \cdot (V_{in} - V_{thr}) \]

The TDC output is:

\[ D_{out} = \frac{t_{delay}}{t_{cell}} \]

Combining:

\[ D_{out} = \frac{1\,\mu s/V}{5\,ns}(V_{in} - V_{thr}) \] \[ D_{out} = 200 \cdot (V_{in} - V_{thr}) \]

docs.title: Voltage Resolution
docs.text:
The effective voltage resolution is:

\[ LSB_V = \frac{t_{cell}}{C/I} \] \[ LSB_V = \frac{5\,ns}{1\,\mu s/V} \] \[ LSB_V = 5\,mV \]

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
\[ N_{bits} \approx \log_2(200) \approx 7.6\,bits \]

The architecture therefore approaches an effective 8-bit resolution.

docs.title: Parasitic Contributions
docs.text:
The delay of each cell is influenced by parasitic capacitances:

\[ t_{cell} \approx R_{eq} C_{load} \]

with:

\[ C_{load} = C_{gate} + C_{wire} + C_{junction} + C_{well} \]

These parasitics impact:

  • delay accuracy
  • matching
  • linearity

docs.title: Mismatch
docs.text: \[ t_{cell,k} = t_{cell} + \Delta t_k \]

docs.title: Metastability
docs.text: Occurs when STOP samples a switching node.

docs.title: Bubble Errors
docs.text:
\[ 111101110000 \]

Corrected with digital logic.

docs.title: PVT Variations
docs.text:
\[ t_{cell} = f(P,V,T) \]

Calibration is required.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The TDC acts as a fine time quantizer with:

  • 5 ns resolution
  • ~1.3 µs range
  • thermometer encoding

Thanks to the optimized VTC, the TDC range is now efficiently utilized, enabling high-resolution conversion.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: The TDC provides time quantization with a resolution of 5 ns over a range of 1.275 µs. Combined with the optimized VTC, the system achieves an effective resolution close to 8 bits, making it suitable for high-resolution time-based ADC architectures.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Voltage-to-Time Converter (VTC) is the core analog block of the Time-Based ADC. Its function is to convert an input voltage \( V_{in} \) into a time delay \( t_{delay} \), which is then quantized by the Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC).

\[ V_{in} \rightarrow t_{delay} \]

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The VTC is based on a sample-and-hold mechanism followed by a controlled discharge of a capacitive node.

flowchart LR Vin([Vin]) --> SW[Sampling Switch] SW --> CAP((VN)) CAP --> COMP{{Comparator}} COMP --> BUF[Buffer Chain] BUF --> OUT([vtc_out]) CAP --> C0[C0] C0 --> GND1[gnd] CAP --> DIS[Current Mirror Discharge] DIS --> GND2[gnd] Thr([Vthr]) --> COMP

docs.title: Sampling Phase
docs.text:
During the tracking phase, the capacitor is charged to the input voltage:

\[ V_N(t_0) = V_{in} \]

docs.title: Conversion Phase
docs.text:
After sampling, the node \( V_N \) is disconnected from the input and discharges through a controlled current source.

\[ \frac{dV_N}{dt} = -\frac{I}{C} \]

docs.title: Threshold Detection
docs.text:
The comparator triggers when:

\[ V_N(t) = V_{thr} \]

Solving:

\[ t_{delay} = \frac{C}{I}(V_{in} - V_{thr}) \]

docs.title: Design Parameters
docs.text:
The VTC is implemented with the following parameters:

Parameter Value Capacitance \( C \) 100 fF Channel length (sampling devices) 4 µm Substrate resistance 50 Ω Current mirror NMOS \(W/L\) 720 nm / 360 nm

docs.title: Design Target
docs.text:
To ensure efficient use of the TDC dynamic range, the VTC is designed to generate delays on the order of microseconds.

This is achieved by reducing the discharge current to:

\[ I \approx 100\,nA \]

docs.title: Voltage-to-Time Gain
docs.text:
Using:

  • \( C = 100\,fF \)
  • \( I = 100\,nA \)
\[ \frac{C}{I} = \frac{100 \times 10^{-15}}{100 \times 10^{-9}} = 1\,\mu s/V \]

Thus:

\[ t_{delay} = 1\,\mu s/V \cdot (V_{in} - V_{thr}) \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• The delay varies linearly with the input voltage
  • Higher input voltage results in longer discharge time
  • The conversion gain is directly controlled by \( C/I \)

The chosen parameters allow the VTC to fully exploit the dynamic range of the TDC.

docs.title: Capacitance
docs.text:
• Larger \( C \) → longer delay → improved resolution
  • Smaller \( C \) → faster conversion → lower power

docs.title: Current Mirror
docs.text:
• Lower current → larger delay → higher resolution
  • Higher current → shorter delay → reduced resolution

docs.title: Device Dimensions
docs.text:
• Long-channel devices improve current stability
  • Proper \( W/L \) sizing ensures accurate current mirroring

docs.title: Non-Ideal Effects
docs.text:
The VTC performance is affected by several non-idealities:

  • Current mirror mismatch
  • Capacitor variation
  • Comparator offset
  • Thermal noise
  • Substrate coupling (not negligible due to 50 Ω resistance)

docs.title: Key Insight
docs.text:
The VTC implements a linear mapping:

\[ t_{delay} \propto V_{in} \]

By properly tuning the ratio \( C/I \), the delay range can be matched to the TDC resolution, enabling efficient time-domain quantization.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The designed VTC provides:

  • A linear voltage-to-time conversion
  • A tunable gain through \( C \) and \( I \)
  • A delay range compatible with the TDC

With the optimized current level, the VTC enables microsecond-scale delays, ensuring that the full TDC dynamic range is utilized and allowing the overall ADC to achieve near 8-bit resolution.
